Where it began

Sreesanth was born in Kothamangalam, Kerala, on 6 February 1983. As a boy he bowled leg-spin, modelling himself on Anil Kumble, who would one day captain him in Tests. He had a habit of firing in yorkers, though, and with his elder brother's encouragement he turned to fast bowling. The MRF Pace Foundation in Chennai took him on.

He made his first-class debut for Kerala in the 2002-03 season and took 22 wickets in seven Ranji Trophy matches. Himachal Pradesh fell victim to a hat-trick of his in November 2004, and a fine Challenger Trophy the next year, where he was player of the series, brought his India call-up.

The player

His Test debut came against England at Nagpur in March 2006, when he took four wickets opening the bowling with Irfan Pathan. His finest hour came at Johannesburg in December 2006. India had just lost a one-day series heavily, but Sreesanth took 5 for 40 with pace and swing, South Africa were bowled out for 84, and India won a Test in South Africa for the first time. He was man of the match.

In 27 Tests from 2006 to 2011 he took 87 wickets, with three five-wicket hauls. In November 2009 at Kanpur he took six in the match against Sri Lanka, five of them in the first innings, as India won by an innings, and his captain, Mahendra Singh Dhoni, rated him among the best reverse-swing bowlers around.

The big occasions

He had a knack for the moments that mattered. At the first T20 World Cup in South Africa in 2007 he removed both Australian openers, Adam Gilchrist and Matthew Hayden, in the semi-final, finishing with 2 for 12. Hayden's wicket turned the match India's way. In the final against Pakistan, with the game slipping, he stood at fine leg and held the catch from Misbah-ul-Haq that won India the trophy. Four years later he was in the squad that won the 2011 World Cup.

He could entertain with the bat too. At Johannesburg in 2006, after the South African fast bowler Andre Nel had tested him with a string of short balls, Sreesanth ran at the next one and hit it straight back over the bowler's head into the stands. He celebrated by whirling his bat and dancing down the pitch.

Away from the middle

In the first Indian Premier League in 2008 only Sohail Tanveer took more wickets than his 18. He later acted in films, and in January 2021 he returned to play for Kerala before retiring from domestic cricket in March 2022.

And finally

He had a rare gift, too: he could keep the seam bolt upright as he let the ball go, something very few bowlers ever master. With that, his pace and his love of a big stage, Sreesanth had the makings of a great fast bowler. Given a longer Test career, he might well have become one. He was particular about his name, too: not S. Sreesanth, he once explained, just Sreesanth.
